title.narrative: Taking on the Beast – Assessing and Mitigating Corruption to Strengthen Health Systems and Improve Health Outcomes in Middle East and North Africa: The Case of Lebanon and Jordan

description.narrative: Objective 1: Define corruption in healthcare in Lebanon and Jordan, identifying acceptable and corrupt practices, as well as the drivers of corrupt behavior. • Activity: Conduct interviews and focus groups with participants from health and community sectors using hypothetical scenarios (vignettes) to explore perceptions of corruption. • Target group: Key stakeholder groups including policymakers, healthcare professionals, and community representatives. • Expected outcomes: A consensus on the definition and manifestations of corruption in each country’s health system and its main drivers, established across a broad range of stakeholders. Objective 2: Identify and prioritize main corruption risks in the health systems of Lebanon and Jordan and highlight areas of integrity or best practices. • Activities: Apply corruption risk assessment methods through a series of steps: o Review existing evidence on health sector corruption in the MENA region. o Conduct a system diagnosis to map structures and analyze points where corruption is likely to occur. o Prioritize identified corruption risks based on their impact and likelihood. o Develop prevention and management options through a consensus-building exercise. • Target group: National-level health systems stakeholders and policymakers. • Expected outcomes: Country-specific corruption risk profiles for each health system, with prioritized risks and management options. Develop toolkits for corruption risk and integrity assessment that are adaptable to each context. Objective 3: Analyze the political factors that shape the adoption and implementation of anti-corruption reforms in Lebanon and Jordan’s health systems. • Activities: Conduct a political economy analysis, gathering data through document reviews, media accounts, and interviews to examine institutional responses to corruption and potential alliances for reform. • Target group: Key stakeholders, including political economists and governance specialists. • Expected outcomes: A comprehensive analysis of the political and institutional factors influencing anti-corruption measures, including timelines for relevant policies. Objective 4: Co-develop and validate scalable, evidence-based anti-corruption strategies and action plans tailored to each country’s context. • Activities: Develop action plans based on findings from previous objectives, focusing on practical and politically feasible strategies. Conduct validation meetings in each country to refine and endorse these plans. • Target group: A diverse group of stakeholders, including government officials, health professionals, NGOs, and development partners. • Expected outcomes: Endorsed, context-appropriate anti-corruption action plans for the health systems of Lebanon and Jordan. Objective 5: Facilitate evidence synthesis, knowledge-sharing, and policy engagement to support anti-corruption efforts in Lebanon, Jordan, and the wider MENA region. • Activities: Use the K2P knowledge translation framework to create products such as policy briefs and citizen briefs, host policy dialogues, and leverage knowledge-sharing platforms. Organize regional dissemination events to promote South-South exchange and build regional capacity for evidence-based policy.

Our project focuses on understanding and addressing corruption risks in health systems, specifically in Lebanon and Jordan in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region. Corruption in healthcare occurs when individuals misuse their power for personal gain rather than prioritizing patient care. This can reduce the efficiency and trustworthiness of health systems, impacting health outcomes and making it harder to reach Universal Health Coverage (ensuring everyone has access to necessary healthcare) and Sustainable Development Goals (global goals for a better and more equitable world). Corruption also weakens a country’s ability to handle health crises, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, and recover afterward. This three-year research program brings together experts from multiple disciplines to identify and address corruption risks in the health systems of Lebanon and Jordan. These countries were chosen because both face significant health system challenges and high levels of corruption, yet offer opportunities to engage key groups ready to fight corruption in healthcare. In both countries, civil society organizations and the public have called for reforms in the health sector. Our research is organized into five main areas, or work packages (WPs) that seek to: first look at what corruption in the health system means to different people and its main drivers in Lebanon and Jordan (WP1); what the most important risks of corruption and vulnerabilities are in their healthcare systems (WP2); and how political factors affect efforts to fight corruption (WP3). Then, it will come up with plans and strategies to address corruption that fit each country's situation (WP4). Finally, it will seek to close the research to policy gap by promoting the use of research emerging from this work to inform policy and practical changes in healthcare systems. Throughout this project, we will work closely with local communities and policymakers to ensure that our findings are locally relevant and can effectively support policy changes. Building skills for local researchers and leaders is a central goal, strengthening their capacity to address corruption in healthcare within the MENA region and beyond. Ultimately, our program aims to improve knowledge, promote action against healthcare corruption, and enhance anticorruption efforts in Lebanon and Jordan, but also to enrich the anticorruption efforts in the MENA region and globally. We also seek to build the skills of local researchers and leaders in the MENA region.

• Expected outcomes: Completed policy briefs, citizen briefs, policy dialogues in each country, and a regional dissemination event. Increased knowledge and action on healthcare corruption in Lebanon, Jordan, and across the MENA region.

• Target group: o Within-country: Policymakers, healthcare organizations and providers, NGOs (working in within the health sector), national anti-corruption agencies and community stakeholders in both Lebanon and Jordan. o Regional: Partner organizations and international stakeholders, including WHO EMRO and Transparency International.

activity-date.narrative: WP1: Conceptualizing health system corruption, its most common manifestations and key drivers specific to Lebanon and Jordan. We will use qualitative methods such as interviews and focus group discussions. Fieldwork will be conducted with the three different groups: national-level stakeholders (e.g. policymakers from the health sector and other relevant government departments, national committees working on anti-corruption, etc.), health professionals (physicians, nurses and managers working in hospitals and primary healthcare centers), and community representatives (patient associations, selected patients, NGOs). Interview and focused-group discussions will cover a number of different topics related to conceptualization of corruption, factors that shape acceptability or not of different corrupt practices, and key drivers of corruption and potential anti-corruption strategies. We have developed and are currently pilot-testing the tools for the interviews and focused group discussions. We have also submitted the study for IRB approval. Additionally, we have mapped the key stakeholders for the interviews and focused-group discussion. We will proceed with data collection in September 2025.

WP2: Assessing health system corruption and integrity risks, and exploring options to address the prioritized risks specific to each study country - Step 1: Stocktaking exercise of evidence on health sector corruption in the Middle East and African (MENA) region. We have registered the scoping review with Open Science Framework. We have completed the title and abstract screening phase and are currently proceeding to full-text screening phase. We have also completed mapping of the legal and administrative landscape for anti-corruption efforts in Lebanon
